jokes.text: I was in the middle of bidding on a bag of bras on eBay.
jokes.setup: Jack summons Liz for an urgent meeting.
jokes.punchline: She was doing something pathetically mundane and specific — bidding on a bag of bras on eBay.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'a bag of bras' is what elevates this beyond a generic 'I was doing something embarrassing' joke. It's perfectly calibrated to Liz's character — practical, unglamorous, and slightly sad. 'Bag' not 'bras' is doing the heavy lifting comedically.

jokes.text: It's not, hon. I saw that in a movie once, but in the movie, the guy was dead.
jokes.setup: Liz asks if the meeting with Hank is a good thing.
jokes.punchline: Pete says he saw that reassurance in a movie, but the character being reassured was dead.
jokes.explanation: Well-structured dark gag. The setup is an innocent reassurance; the punchline flips it to horror without being overwrought. The delivery is casual, which amplifies the darkness.

jokes.text: Nice tie, Jack. / How long have you been there? / I was sitting in that chair a minute ago. / Nope. That was me. / What can I say? I smell like leather.
jokes.setup: Jack and Liz are surprised to find Hank Hooper already in the room.
jokes.punchline: Hank was already sitting in the chair Jack thought he was sitting in — the two men smell alike, which Hank delivers as a cheerful non-explanation.
jokes.explanation: The exchange works as character establishment for Hank — he's affably confounding. 'I smell like leather' as an explanation is absurdist and lands because it's delivered with total confidence.

jokes.text: Well, I'll be Bake McBrided. I know a Philly gal when I hug one.
jokes.setup: Hank meets Liz Lemon for the first time.
jokes.punchline: Hank uses the made-up folksy expression 'I'll be Bake McBrided' and immediately hugs her, identifying her as a Philly gal by the hug.
jokes.explanation: 'Bake McBrided' is a perfectly invented nonsense proper-noun exclamation. It sounds like it could be a real Pennsylvania Dutch expression, which makes it funnier than a purely random word. Strong character comedy for Hank.

jokes.text: Without Tracy, your show is like my cholesterol. The numbers are killing me.
jokes.setup: Hank is about to deliver bad news about TGS's ratings.
jokes.punchline: He compares the show to his cholesterol — the numbers are killing him — making a health complaint do double duty as a cancellation threat.
jokes.explanation: Elegant double meaning. The simile connects Hank's folksy personality (talking about his health) with the professional stakes simultaneously. Efficient and well-constructed.

jokes.text: Got on Wikipedia this week.
jokes.setup: Jack is trying to convince Hank not to cancel TGS by citing good media buzz.
jokes.punchline: 'Getting on Wikipedia' is offered as a major PR achievement, underlining how desperate and low the bar has fallen.
jokes.explanation: Concise and sharp. The comedy is all in the delivery and context — Wikipedia in 2011 was a cultural shorthand for irrelevance or minimal achievement. Four words, big laugh potential.

jokes.text: You want to cancel the only show on your network starring a 42-year-old woman? A show that is number one in its time slot among men 18 to 49 months left in prison?
jokes.setup: Liz challenges Hank about canceling TGS, citing its time-slot ranking.
jokes.punchline: 'Men 18 to 49 months left in prison' — the demographic descriptor is revealed to be a prison sentence, not an age range.
jokes.explanation: This is a near-perfect joke. The setup mimics the real TV industry language of demographic ratings ('men 18 to 49') and then subverts it mid-phrase so that '49' is not an age but months. The joke arrives late enough in the sentence that the misdirection has full effect. It simultaneously lambastes TGS's actual viewership and skewers TV industry jargon. Highly quotable, structurally tight, genuinely original. One of the episode's best.

jokes.text: I thought this company was a family, but I guess it's that Austrian family and I am the girl in the basement, and you are the dad who has been brutally-- Thank you, Lemon.
jokes.setup: Liz is making an impassioned speech about being let down by the company.
jokes.punchline: The 'family' metaphor escalates to the Josef Fritzl case (Austrian father who imprisoned his daughter) before Jack cuts her off mid-sentence.
jokes.explanation: The joke works on multiple levels: Liz's tendency to escalate corporate complaints into increasingly inappropriate metaphors, the specific choice of the Fritzl case as the endpoint, and Jack's perfectly-timed interruption that implies he's heard this before. The cut-off is funnier than any completed sentence would have been. 30 Rock's darkness at its best.

jokes.text: You get one more shot. Just like the army doctor said to me after my weekend in Okinawa.
jokes.setup: Hank gives TGS one more chance.
jokes.punchline: He compares it to an army doctor giving him 'one more shot' after a weekend in Okinawa — implying something medically alarming happened.
jokes.explanation: Classic dark subversive digression from a seemingly wholesome character. 'Okinawa' does a lot of geographic work — it implies a specific kind of R&R behavior without spelling it out. Efficient and well-timed as a scene button.

jokes.text: They're mean. Jack Welch once smacked a pretzel out of my hand at the Super Bowl.
jokes.setup: Hank notes that Jack ended up at Kabletown instead of running GE, implying GE people are difficult.
jokes.punchline: Hank's evidence for GE being 'mean' is Jack Welch slapping a pretzel out of his hand at the Super Bowl — a hilariously specific and petty act.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'a pretzel' and 'at the Super Bowl' makes this. Jack Welch is a real GE titan, which adds a satirical bite. The image of a powerful CEO petulantly smacking a snack out of a rival's hands is absurd and perfectly scaled. Hank narrating it as plain fact amplifies the comedy.

jokes.text: Is Tracy back? I'd hate to think I just lied to Hank. Geez, I'll get it done. You know I'll do whatever it takes. Lemon-style. [music cue: 'Everybody Dance Now']
jokes.setup: Liz says she'll handle getting Tracy back 'Lemon-style.'
jokes.punchline: The phrase 'Lemon-style' triggers a C+C Music Factory sting, immediately undercut because Liz's methods are famously chaotic and ineffective.
jokes.explanation: The self-aggrandizing music sting after 'Lemon-style' is funny precisely because Liz is the least badass person. It's a brief but well-executed ironic moment.

jokes.text: You gonna get me another sandwich or I'm gonna cut your face up so bad you'll have a chin. I will waste you! You'll have to go through this old bastard first.
jokes.setup: We see Tracy Jordan being volatile, apparently in character as D'Jeffrey or just being Tracy.
jokes.punchline: 'Cut your face up so bad you'll have a chin' — threatening to give someone a chin by slashing them is a hilariously inverted threat.
jokes.explanation: The threat of giving someone a chin via facial laceration is an extremely original comedic inversion. Most threats promise to take something away — this one promises to add a body feature through violence. Genuinely inventive.

jokes.text: And I don't really think it's fair for me to be on a jury because I'm a hologram.
jokes.setup: Tracy is being erratic and delusional in various ways.
jokes.punchline: He believes he's a hologram and cites this as a disqualification from jury duty.
jokes.explanation: Pure Tracyism. The logic that a hologram can't serve on a jury is internally consistent in its absurdity. It also works as meta-commentary on celebrity delusion. The offhand delivery amid the other chaos makes it land harder.

jokes.text: He feels like a Bartram's Scrub-Hairstreak trying to crawl back into its silky cocoon. Which is a butterfly metaphor, by the way, and not, as I first thought, a list of African-American hair products.
jokes.setup: Liz is relaying Tracy's own metaphor for his state of mind.
jokes.punchline: She clarifies it's a butterfly metaphor and not a list of Black hair products — admitting she initially misread it that way.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. It works on three layers: (1) 'Bartram's Scrub-Hairstreak' is a real but obscure butterfly name that sounds like a product, (2) Liz's admission that she initially misread it is a perfect character beat — her whiteness and cultural obliviousness made her parse it wrong, (3) the correction itself is funnier than any original joke would be. Highly quotable, structurally elegant, and shows tremendous craft. Comparable in quality to the 8.0 anchor.

jokes.text: Well you just need to turn the beautiful butterfly back into a drunk, incompetent caterpillar.
jokes.setup: Liz used a butterfly metaphor for Tracy's artistic transformation.
jokes.punchline: Jack inverts the typical butterfly metaphor — instead of aspiring to become a butterfly, they need to reverse the process to make Tracy 'a drunk, incompetent caterpillar.'
jokes.explanation: Brilliant callback and inversion. Jack weaponizes the metaphor to articulate the show's absurd premise — they need to make Tracy worse again. 'Drunk, incompetent caterpillar' is a spectacular phrase. The economy is perfect; the inversion is precise.

jokes.text: Jesus was black!
jokes.setup: Tracy is being prepped for a morning show interview and a host mentions being at Mar-a-Lago.
jokes.punchline: Tracy's non-sequitur response to an anodyne question is 'Jesus was black!' — an instant controversy-generating declaration.
jokes.explanation: Maximum economy — three words do enormous work, establishing the scheme (make Tracy offensive), the character (Tracy goes straight for controversy), and the comedy (the non-sequitur response to a mundane premise). The contrast with the Mar-a-Lago small talk is the structure.

jokes.text: In 100 shows, we've done Pam 107 times.
jokes.setup: The crew celebrates the 100th episode milestone after doing a 'Pam the overly-confident obese woman' sketch.
jokes.punchline: They've done the Pam sketch 107 times across only 100 episodes — meaning they repeated it more than once per episode on average.
jokes.explanation: The arithmetic here is the joke — 107 > 100 implies they do Pam multiple times in some episodes, which is a savage commentary on the laziness of sketch TV. Also establishes Pam as a running gag within the show, which pays off at episode's end.

jokes.text: Um, that wasn't me. There used to be another guy. I don't think so.
jokes.setup: Jenna references memories from the first five years of TGS, addressing Danny.
jokes.punchline: Danny points out he wasn't there from the start; Jenna dismisses the idea there was ever anyone else.
jokes.explanation: A meta joke about cast turnover — Jenna simply refusing to acknowledge previous cast members exists. Character-specific and works as quiet backstage commentary.

jokes.text: I will choke you to death with your boyfriend's wig!
jokes.setup: Danny brings up fond memories of the past five years with Jenna.
jokes.punchline: Jenna's response is a violently specific threat involving strangling him with someone else's hairpiece.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'your boyfriend's wig' as the murder weapon is what makes this. Generic threats are weak; this one implies a whole secondary storyline (Danny's boyfriend, the wig) while being outrageously violent. Pure Jenna.

jokes.text: Give me back my man, bitch!
jokes.setup: Jenna continues her tirade at Danny about past memories.
jokes.punchline: She demands her man back from Danny — confirming Danny is with Jenna's ex.
jokes.explanation: Escalation of the prior threat that pays off the 'boyfriend' detail. Less original than the wig joke but provides necessary context. Functions as a tag.

jokes.text: I'll never forget what you said to me after that first show, miss Maroney. / Terrific show, ma'am. If I know anything about television, The Girlie Show is a hit. / Oh, please. If this turkey goes 100 episodes, I'll have your baby.
jokes.setup: Kenneth reminisces about what Jenna said after the first show.
jokes.punchline: Jenna's 'encouraging' words were actually a sarcastic bet that she'd have Kenneth's baby if the show succeeded — which now inadvertently creates a plot obligation.
jokes.explanation: This joke sets up an entire subplot with great efficiency. The contrast between Kenneth's sincere warmth and Jenna's savage dismissal is classic, and the callback bet (baby for 100 episodes) is absurd enough to be the episode's B-plot engine. The 'I was so young' reflection adds a layer of genuine comedic pathos.

jokes.text: Wait. I saw that. How? Am I dead?
jokes.setup: Kenneth shows Jenna a flashback/recording of what she said five years ago.
jokes.punchline: Jenna's first instinct when seeing footage of her past self is to wonder if she's dead — as if the only explanation for seeing yourself on screen is haunting.
jokes.explanation: Jenna's narcissism and solipsism make her genuinely incapable of understanding recorded video without assuming supernatural circumstances. Character-specific and quick.

jokes.text: Well, it's been 100 episodes. I better lay you across my grandmother's lap in the mating shed.
jokes.setup: Kenneth is responding to Jenna's baby bet from the flashback.
jokes.punchline: Kenneth's rural Kentucky folkways emerge: 'the mating shed' and 'grandmother's lap' as part of the conception ritual — suggesting deeply strange rural customs.
jokes.explanation: An outstanding Kenneth joke. The 'mating shed' is an inspired piece of world-building for his character's bizarre rural background. 'Grandmother's lap' as part of the ritual adds a layer of wrongness that's pure cringe comedy. It's character-specific — only Kenneth could deliver this with sincere sweetness and make it funnier.

jokes.text: I wish. Albinos get to be watchers in the mating shed.
jokes.setup: Jenna calls Kenneth an albino goon.
jokes.punchline: Kenneth wistfully wishes he were albino because albinos have a specific ceremonial role in the mating shed.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best joke. It expands the 'mating shed' mythology with perfect economy — albinos serve a specific ceremonial function — and Kenneth delivers it with wistful sincerity, as if he's genuinely sad about his non-albino status. The callback to joke #24 deepens the running gag. The joke builds an entire absurd rural world in one line. Exceptional character integration: only Kenneth, only this show. Comparable to the 8.0+ anchor examples.

jokes.text: The only thing I want latched to my funbags are celebrity DJs.
jokes.setup: Someone suggests Jenna would make a wonderful parent who could nurse a baby.
jokes.punchline: Jenna prefers celebrity DJs to babies on her body.
jokes.explanation: The word 'funbags' is funny; 'celebrity DJs' as the preferred alternative to an infant is funnier. Pure Jenna: sexually forward, fame-obsessed, anti-maternal. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: You could sing the baby to sleep and tell it fairy tales and act out all the witch parts.
jokes.setup: Kenneth is earnestly trying to convince Jenna she'd be a good mother.
jokes.punchline: His specific suggestion — she could act out all the witch parts — implies he knows Jenna is best suited for villainous roles, delivered with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: Kenneth's sincere belief that Jenna's talent is in playing witches — delivered as a compliment — is a perfect character beat. The joke is in what Kenneth doesn't realize he's revealing about his opinion of Jenna.

jokes.text: You're serious? You albino goon.
jokes.setup: Kenneth sincerely compliments Jenna's potential as a mother.
jokes.punchline: Jenna's response is to call him an 'albino goon' — an insult that reveals she perceives his sincerity as threatening.
jokes.explanation: Short but effective reaction beat. 'Albino goon' is a specific enough insult to be funny; the pivot from maternal warmth to insult is very Jenna.

jokes.text: A picture of you in Us Weekly next to Natalie Portman in the same maternity outfit. 'Who wore it best?' / I did. I wore it best.
jokes.setup: Liz imagines Jenna pregnant and pictures the tabloid coverage.
jokes.punchline: Jenna immediately asserts she wore the maternity outfit better than Natalie Portman — without a beat of self-doubt.
jokes.explanation: The 'Who wore it best?' tabloid format is instantly recognizable, and Jenna's unironic self-declaration is perfect. The specificity of Natalie Portman (who was pregnant and Oscar-winning at the time) makes it timely and sharp. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: All right. Ride it straight to hell! / Here come the roofies. / Where's my Mac and cheese? / And we've had some good times. / Who wants-- my puddings!
jokes.setup: Liz is trying to give a pep talk by recalling their darkest moments.
jokes.punchline: The 'bad times' montage consists of three rapid, increasingly specific and absurd crises: a suicidal declaration, someone roofying the staff, and a Mac and cheese emergency.
jokes.explanation: Rapid-fire montage comedy. Each of the three 'bad times' snippets is absurd and specific, building to a comic rhythm. The parallel 'good times' montage with 'my puddings!' as its climax is the payoff — puddings are a 'good time.' Great structural use of parallel construction.

jokes.text: Tonight, TGS will not be the worst thing on television. It'll be John Stossel.
jokes.setup: Liz gives her pep talk, saying TGS won't be the worst thing on TV.
jokes.punchline: She names John Stossel specifically as the thing that will be worse — a real ABC/Fox journalist used as a punchline.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'John Stossel' rather than a generic bad show is the whole joke. It's a real name-drop with genuine satirical edge. Works as a pep talk button and a dig at a real person, which 30 Rock does regularly and well.

jokes.text: Why now? On my last day before retirement. / That's my girl. We're getting married when I get out of here. / Why am I showing you guys this? It's gonna jinx everything. Plus you're a couple of pervs.
jokes.setup: A maintenance worker discovers a gas leak on his last day before retirement.
jokes.punchline: He shows coworkers a photo of his fiancée — immediately calling it a jinx and also calling them pervs for looking at it.
jokes.explanation: The 'one day from retirement' cop movie cliché is being lampshaded deliberately — the worker is superstitious about jinxing it. 'Plus you're a couple of pervs' as the secondary reason not to show the photo is an excellent tag. Parody of a genre convention.

jokes.text: Who's up there? TGS? Isn't that show already half-dead?
jokes.setup: Workers realize the gas leak is heading toward the sixth floor where TGS tapes.
jokes.punchline: One worker casually notes TGS is 'already half-dead,' a real-world observation delivered with total disinterest.
jokes.explanation: A functional meta-commentary joke from an outsider character. Gets the point across but not particularly crafted.

jokes.text: Do you know what I find fascinating? Mystery novels written by janitors?
jokes.setup: Liz rushes in to tell Jack about the gas leak.
jokes.punchline: Jack interrupts with a rhetorical question about what he finds fascinating, which he immediately answers with a random absurdity before anyone can respond.
jokes.explanation: Jack's rhetorical non-sequitur about janitor mystery novels is a nice character beat — he controls every conversation, even the ones he doesn't want to have, by derailing them with absurdity.

jokes.text: See? I got a new hair. It's white and it hurts, but--
jokes.setup: Jack is insisting he has many other things going on in his life besides TGS.
jokes.punchline: His example of 'other things going on' is a single new white hair — which he notes hurts.
jokes.explanation: The specificity that the hair 'hurts' is what elevates this. It's a pathetic example of Jack having a life, delivered with Jack's characteristic dignity, and the physical detail of it hurting adds absurdist texture.

jokes.text: Prolonged exposure could lead to incapacitation or even death. Other possible side effects include hallucinations, revelation of secrets, telling of truths, flashbacks, headaches, nostalgia.
jokes.setup: Liz is describing the effects of the gas leak like a pharmaceutical ad.
jokes.punchline: The side effects list includes 'revelation of secrets, telling of truths, flashbacks, nostalgia' — which are exactly the tropes of a 100th episode clip show, making this meta-commentary on the episode's own structure.
jokes.explanation: This is a masterclass in meta-comedy. The gas leak is the episode's structural device (causing flashbacks, hallucinations, nostalgic conversations), and this joke explicitly names it as such — 'hallucinations, revelation of secrets, telling of truths, flashbacks, nostalgia' is the checklist for a 100th episode. It earns the episode's premise while skewering the genre. Genuinely sophisticated.

jokes.text: I refuse to have long, gas-induced conversations with any of you people.
jokes.setup: Jack is told about the gas leak's side effects (including inducing conversations).
jokes.punchline: Jack explicitly refuses to participate in the episode's conceit — the gas-induced conversations that are the entire premise.
jokes.explanation: Jack refusing to participate in the episode's plot device while the episode's plot device immediately starts happening to him is perfect meta-comedy. It's a callback to his character's self-awareness, and it's funnier because it fails immediately.

jokes.text: I can't believe it's been 100 shows. More like 100 little strokes.
jokes.setup: The 100th episode milestone is being celebrated.
jokes.punchline: Pete, perpetually ground down by the show, compares the episodes to mini-strokes he's been suffering.
jokes.explanation: Concise, dark, and perfectly Pete. His broken spirit is his defining characteristic, and '100 little strokes' is a memorable formulation. Strong economy — four words replace what could have been a whole monologue about being worn down.

jokes.text: Oh, life was so much simpler back then. I had a boyfriend. Dennis. Sure, he was an idiot, but he made great chili, and he didn't care if I watched TV during sex.
jokes.setup: Liz is nostalgically thinking about life before Jack and Tracy.
jokes.punchline: Her fond memories of Dennis boil down to: he made chili and didn't mind her watching TV during sex — the bar for a good relationship is depressingly low.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character comedy. The list of Dennis's virtues is two things, and both are perfectly calibrated to Liz: food (chili) and passive entertainment (TV during sex). It's a simultaneously sympathetic and savage self-portrait. 'He didn't care if I watched TV during sex' is a legendary Liz Lemon line.

jokes.text: The gas is not affecting me yet, so I can lead you to safety. Just follow these... Troll penises! Oh, God! What have I done?
jokes.setup: Pete declares he is unaffected by the gas and will lead everyone to safety.
jokes.punchline: Mid-sentence he hallucinates 'Troll penises' and immediately collapses into self-recrimination.
jokes.explanation: The joke structure is perfect: build up (I'm fine, follow me), instant collapse (Troll penises!), self-awareness (Oh God, what have I done?). 'Troll penises' as the first hallucination is an inspired specific choice. The three-beat rhythm is textbook 30 Rock joke construction.

jokes.text: Tracy! Tracy. Tracy? / Why don't you shut your mouth, back that ass up and make me a sandwich?
jokes.setup: Tracy is welcomed on a morning show but is still in character as D'Jeffrey, the abusive Oscar-winning role.
jokes.punchline: His response to the warm welcome is an immediate verbal assault demanding a sandwich.
jokes.explanation: The escalating 'Tracy!' greetings followed by an aggressive non-sequitur is solid Tracy comedy. The character-in-character (D'Jeffrey bleeding into Tracy) is a fun structural wrinkle.

jokes.text: I lied to all you ugly white ladies. I didn't go to Africa. I was hiding in a warehouse in Queens, watching vintage pornography.
jokes.setup: The morning show hosts are praising Tracy for his post-Oscar trip to Africa to reconnect with his roots.
jokes.punchline: He admits he lied — he was watching vintage porn in Queens the whole time.
jokes.explanation: This is a great Tracy joke. The contrast between the noble Africa narrative and the Queens warehouse pornography is perfectly scaled. 'Ugly white ladies' as the address to morning show hosts is both offensive and precise. 'Vintage pornography' adds an unnecessary and therefore funnier specificity.

jokes.text: No! It's unbrave! You should hate me!
jokes.setup: The morning show hosts call Tracy 'brave' for walking away from success.
jokes.punchline: Tracy insists it's 'unbrave' and demands that they hate him — the opposite of what anyone seeking approval would say.
jokes.explanation: 'Unbrave' as a coinage is excellent — it's not a real word but it's immediately clear and more emphatic than 'cowardly.' The desperation of demanding to be hated makes Tracy's predicament funny and weirdly sympathetic.

jokes.text: It's new haircuts, but you can make salads with them.
jokes.setup: Tracy asks what 'hair make-unders' means.
jokes.punchline: They're haircuts from which you can also make salads — a genuinely inexplicable answer.
jokes.explanation: Pure absurdism — the explanation creates more confusion than it resolves. The matter-of-fact delivery is the key. Short and effective.

jokes.text: A true artist... He feels things we don't.
jokes.setup: Tracy has just admitted he lied about Africa and watched vintage porn in Queens.
jokes.punchline: The hosts respond by praising Tracy as a 'true artist who feels things we don't' — completely missing the point.
jokes.explanation: Satire of celebrity media sycophancy — no matter what Tracy says, the hosts interpret it as artistic depth. Functions as a reaction beat that amplifies the prior joke.

jokes.text: Frank, what is this? 'Broken eyboard alk show'? / I write what I know. Also I broke my keyboard.
jokes.setup: Liz reviews sketch pitches and finds one with a garbled title.
jokes.punchline: Frank explains he broke his keyboard — so his pitch is literally titled with missing letters from a broken 'K' and 'T' key.
jokes.explanation: Cleverly constructed wordplay. 'Broken eyboard alk show' is missing the 'K' and 'T', which is both a visual gag (seeing the garbled text on cue cards) and a character joke (Frank pitching something he literally can't spell). Two explanations collapse into one: his subject matter AND his equipment failure.

jokes.text: I'm so beloved, I can do no wrong. Now everyone's after me. Unicef, the Gates Foundation. And what is Farm Aid? Is it a drink? Is it a drug? Is it a bandage you put on a barn?
jokes.setup: Tracy reports that his plan to make people hate him has completely backfired.
jokes.punchline: He lists the organizations now pursuing him (Unicef, Gates Foundation), then completely doesn't know what Farm Aid is, offering three wrong answers in rapid succession.
jokes.explanation: 'Is it a drink? Is it a drug? Is it a bandage you put on a barn?' — the three guesses escalate perfectly, with 'bandage you put on a barn' being both the most absurd and most logical of the three. Highly quotable and perfectly Tracy. The callback to his beloved status is well-structured.

jokes.text: See, that's the kind of lazy stand-up I'll never do again.
jokes.setup: Tracy has just delivered an absurdist 'Farm Aid' riff and immediately recognizes it as lazy stand-up.
jokes.punchline: By calling out his own riff as 'lazy stand-up he'll never do again,' he's both self-aware AND proving his comedy instincts are gone — the meta-awareness is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant meta-joke. Tracy correctly identifies the Farm Aid bit as lazy stand-up, then declares he won't do it anymore — making the declaration itself the punchline to the bit he just did. It's a self-canceling joke that also advances the plot (Tracy has become too self-aware to be funny). Extremely clever.

jokes.text: F-u, l.l. Spells 'full,' because you're full of BS, Liz Lemon.
jokes.setup: Tracy is angry at Liz and wants to tell her off.
jokes.punchline: He spells out 'F-U, L.L.' — his version of 'full of BS' using her initials, delivered as if it's a devastating burn.
jokes.explanation: Tracy's playful phonetic spelling of an insult using her initials is endearing and funny. The self-explanation ('spells full') is the character: he's proud of the wordplay and wants to be sure she gets it.

jokes.text: Be like Michael McDonald and take it to the streets.
jokes.setup: Liz is advising Tracy to take his campaign to be publicly hated directly to the public.
jokes.punchline: She references Michael McDonald (Doobie Brothers singer) and his song 'Takin' It to the Streets' as a serious strategic recommendation.
jokes.explanation: A quick pop culture reference that works as a throwaway. The absurdity of using Michael McDonald as a strategic model is mild but functional.

jokes.text: I think Bono got in my limo.
jokes.setup: Tracy is venting about his problems being too beloved.
jokes.punchline: He adds, as an afterthought, that Bono may have gotten into his limo — treating a celebrity intrusion as a minor inconvenience.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — seven words, completely throwaway, treating Bono's apparent intrusion as a minor annoyance in a list of bigger problems. The nonchalance is the whole joke.

jokes.text: No. And I wasn't even drinking anything.
jokes.setup: Jenna asks Liz if she thinks she'd be a good mother.
jokes.punchline: Liz says no, then adds she wasn't even drinking — implying that saying 'no' to Jenna sometimes requires liquid courage.
jokes.explanation: Clean and efficient. The comedy is in the addendum — Liz's honesty with Jenna is so unusual that she notes the absence of alcohol as remarkable. Character-specific for both women.

jokes.text: Being pregnant is a great excuse for why I stopped working instead of the truth. I'm in my 40s, very difficult, and not that good at playing La Realite.
jokes.setup: Jenna explains why she wants a baby.
jokes.punchline: Her real reason is that she wants cover for why her career is ending — and she admits she's 'not that good' at a reality show role.
jokes.explanation: Brutal self-awareness from Jenna — she knows she's difficult and not that talented but frames having a baby as a PR strategy rather than facing the truth. The specificity of 'La Realite' as the reality show makes it feel lived-in.

jokes.text: You will have a child. Who will grow up to be a little gay fancy man.
jokes.setup: Liz is trying to talk Jenna out of having a baby.
jokes.punchline: Her prediction for Jenna's hypothetical child is that he'll be 'a little gay fancy man' — implying Jenna would raise a stereotypically flamboyant child.
jokes.explanation: 'Little gay fancy man' is a vivid and specific phrase. The joke relies on the implication that Jenna's showbiz world would inevitably produce this type of child, which is both a commentary on Jenna's environment and a quick character portrait.

jokes.text: Well, good luck finding a man willing to ride that crazy train.
jokes.setup: Jenna says she'll find a man willing to father her child.
jokes.punchline: Liz's response uses the 'crazy train' metaphor — implying Jenna's personality would deter any potential father.
jokes.explanation: 'Crazy train' is a well-worn idiom and doesn't add much beyond the existing characterization. Functional but not particularly crafted.

jokes.text: I'll have you know I talked with a man this morning who thinks I'd be a wonderful mother. / He must be an idiot. / He is an idiot.
jokes.setup: Jenna says a man told her she'd be a wonderful mother; Liz calls him an idiot.
jokes.punchline: Jenna instantly agrees — 'He is an idiot' — confirming both Kenneth's stupidity and that she still values his opinion.
jokes.explanation: The structure is impeccable: setup, Liz's prediction, Jenna's confirmation. The joke works because it subverts the expected defensive response — instead of defending Kenneth, Jenna agrees he's an idiot, which makes her reliance on his opinion even funnier. Crisp three-beat structure.

jokes.text: I'm Jack Donaghy, CEO of General Electric. / You were Jack Donaghy. You were magnificent.
jokes.setup: Jack hallucinates an alternate-universe version of himself — 'Sideways Jack' — who succeeded at GE.
jokes.punchline: Sideways Jack says 'You were magnificent' — past tense — when Jack introduces himself as CEO of GE.
jokes.explanation: The alternate-universe Jack device is a perfect vehicle for Jack's central tension (TV vs. corporate ambition). The past-tense 'were magnificent' is devastating and precisely placed. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: I run the General. I own an NFL team. I guest-starred on Entourage.
jokes.setup: Sideways Jack lists his accomplishments from the alternate universe.
jokes.punchline: The list escalates from running GE to owning an NFL team to... guest-starring on Entourage, which is hilariously deflating as a final achievement.
jokes.explanation: The list is perfectly structured: two genuinely impressive achievements, then 'I guest-starred on Entourage' as the apex, which is brilliant because it reveals that even this hyper-successful Jack defines himself by celebrity proximity. The anti-climax is the point. Entourage was still airing at the time and was synonymous with a certain kind of male ego. Exceptional economy and structure.

jokes.text: I'll tell you what I don't do. Wear a striped tie with a striped shirt. / It's called 'Power Clashing' and I do it because I can. / I wore this on the January cover of Meetings magazine. / We made the cover during meetings history month? / I made the cover.
jokes.setup: Jack criticizes Sideways Jack's fashion choice; Sideways Jack defends it.
jokes.punchline: 'Meetings magazine' and 'meetings history month' exist as peak achievement markers, which is absurdly specific and deflating for such a powerful man.
jokes.explanation: 'Meetings magazine' and 'meetings history month' are invented institutions that feel plausible in the corporate world, which is what makes them great. The correction 'I made the cover' (not 'we') is a perfect character beat showing Sideways Jack's ego. 'Power Clashing' is an excellent coinage. Multiple jokes firing simultaneously.

jokes.text: She became your focus at the expense of your own ambition. You should have realized within a week that Lemon was a black hole, unworthy of our mentorship.
jokes.setup: Sideways Jack is diagnosing why regular Jack failed to reach his potential.
jokes.punchline: 'Lemon was a black hole, unworthy of our mentorship' — using a physics metaphor to dismiss Liz, while 'our mentorship' implies Jack's narcissism includes his alternate selves.
jokes.explanation: 'Lemon was a black hole' works as both a physics metaphor and a pun on her name. 'Unworthy of our mentorship' — the plural 'our' including both Jacks — is a funny narcissistic detail.

jokes.text: Are you building factories in Bangalore? Are you dining in the Palin White House? No. You're approving TGS wrap gifts. Baseball caps with stupid sayings from the show written on them. What the hell is a 'Pwomp'?
jokes.setup: Sideways Jack is listing what Jack should be doing vs. what he actually does.
jokes.punchline: 'The Palin White House' as a casual reference to an alternate timeline plus the anti-climactic pivot to wrap gifts ending with 'what the hell is a Pwomp?'
jokes.explanation: 'The Palin White House' lands hard as a casual alternate-reality aside — implying in Sideways Jack's world, Sarah Palin is president, and that's just where Jack dines. Then the plunge from that grandiosity to baseball caps and 'Pwomp' is a devastating anti-climax. The mystery of 'Pwomp' (answered: two fat people...) is the tag.

jokes.text: What the hell is a 'Pwomp'? / It's when two fat people-- / I don't care!
jokes.setup: Sideways Jack demands to know what 'Pwomp' means.
jokes.punchline: Jack starts to explain it (implying it's a graphic sound effect for obese people doing something), and Sideways Jack cuts him off — he doesn't actually want to know.
jokes.explanation: The interrupted explanation is funnier than any completed version could be. The setup implies something crude; the cutoff denies resolution while confirming the implication. Three lines, maximum comedy. Also a callback to Pam's sketch earlier in the episode.

jokes.text: The real Jack Donaghy could handle a little gas leak!
jokes.setup: The gas leak has spread and Jack is told to evacuate.
jokes.punchline: Sideways Jack's parting shot is that 'the real Jack Donaghy' could handle gas, which is both a taunt and absurd — surviving a gas leak is not a measure of greatness.
jokes.explanation: A scene button that captures the absurdity of the whole Sideways Jack sequence. The taunt is inherently silly, which is appropriate for the conclusion of a hallucination.

jokes.text: I am a Jedi!
jokes.setup: Jack is wandering through the gas-affected hallways.
jokes.punchline: He randomly declares himself a Jedi — a non-sequitur hallucination that suggests his gas-induced mental state.
jokes.explanation: A quick visual moment — Jack's dignified bearing combined with a Star Wars delusion is inherently funny. Not sophisticated but delivers a laugh.

jokes.text: Hey, look. Tracy Jordan is ironically reappropriating his bad past behavior as a commentary on Fitzgerald's dictum that there are no second acts in American life.
jokes.setup: Tracy is acting out publicly in a way that's meant to make people hate him.
jokes.punchline: Random bystanders interpret his bad behavior as sophisticated literary commentary on F. Scott Fitzgerald.
jokes.explanation: This joke is simultaneously a satire of celebrity culture (any behavior is reinterpreted as intentional art), literary pretension (the Fitzgerald reference is genuine and apt), and Tracy's predicament. The fact that the bystanders are right in a meta sense — Tracy IS negotiating a second act — makes it even smarter.

jokes.text: I want to take a picture of him with my old-fashioned camera. / No! No! / Ah! / Help! I can't swim! / He just pulled me out of the water and said, 'Don't tell anyone I did this.' / I didn't even get a chance to congratulate him on his Oscar. / Modesty and heroism. Two words forever synonymous with Tracy Jordan.
jokes.setup: Tracy attacks a bystander's camera but accidentally saves the person from drowning.
jokes.punchline: The rescue is immediately spun by media as modesty and heroism, further cementing Tracy's beloved status.
jokes.explanation: The escalation structure is excellent — Tracy tries to destroy his image, accidentally becomes heroic, tells the victim not to tell anyone (adding 'modesty'), and the media labels him a hero. 'Modesty and heroism. Two words forever synonymous with Tracy Jordan' is a brilliant ironic kicker.

jokes.text: Lutz, what are you working on? / Breathing through my mouth so I don't smell the throw-up on my shirt.
jokes.setup: Liz asks the writing staff what they're working on.
jokes.punchline: Lutz's sole activity is mouth-breathing to avoid smelling his own vomit-covered shirt.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Lutz joke — he's always the most pathetic writer and his response confirms it. The specificity of 'mouth-breathing to avoid the vomit on his own shirt' is disgusting and funny in equal measure.

jokes.text: I would take my shirt off, but I visited my rescue chimp for his birthday last week, and another chimp got mad and bit my nipple off. He played with it, and then he kissed it, and then he ate it.
jokes.setup: Lutz is explaining why he can't remove his vomit-covered shirt.
jokes.punchline: A rival chimp ate his nipple at a birthday party — and the specific detail of the chimp 'playing with it, then kissing it, then eating it' makes it horrifying and hilarious.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes for sheer commitment and escalation. Each beat in the three-part sequence (played, kissed, ate) is funnier than the last, with 'kissed it' being the unexpected middle step that makes the eating the inevitable conclusion. The chimp birthday party as context is inspired. The complete non-sequitur from vomit-shirt to chimp-ate-nipple is perfect 30 Rock digression comedy.

jokes.text: Cerie, did you not bring my computer down? / You said you were writing. I've only seen you use that computer to look at pictures of Nate Berkus.
jokes.setup: Liz demands her computer.
jokes.punchline: Cerie points out Liz only uses it to look at photos of Nate Berkus (Oprah's interior designer/TV personality) — implying a parasocial obsession.
jokes.explanation: Nate Berkus is a specific enough reference to be funny — he's not a conventional sex symbol, which makes Liz's obsession oddly specific and therefore very Liz. Cerie calling her out is a nice role reversal.

jokes.text: Ah! Pwomp!
jokes.setup: Liz reacts to something (presumably an embarrassing moment with Nate Berkus).
jokes.punchline: She involuntarily shouts 'Pwomp!' — the unexplained TGS sketch catchphrase — proving she knows what it means.
jokes.explanation: Genius callback. The word 'Pwomp' was defined as 'when two fat people--' earlier and never completed. Liz shouting it as a reaction implies she knows exactly what it means and that it applies to this situation. Maximum comedy from maximum economy — one word pays off two prior setups.

jokes.text: Five years of my business life wasted, and I'm still supposed to hold your hand. Your wet, yet somehow flaky hand.
jokes.setup: Jack is complaining about Liz still needing his help.
jokes.punchline: He adds a specific, unpleasant physical description of her hand — 'wet, yet somehow flaky.'
jokes.explanation: The paradox of 'wet, yet somehow flaky' is both a specific physical joke and a commentary on Liz's general state of unglamorous being. The 'somehow' is the key word — even Jack is confused by this hand.

jokes.text: Sort of feel like you're gonna say Leno.
jokes.setup: Jack is building to revealing whose fault his career failure is.
jokes.punchline: Liz guesses Jay Leno — a reasonable NBC-workplace target for blame — before Jack says it's her.
jokes.explanation: A quick topical gag — at the time, the Leno/Conan late night wars were recent. Works as a misdirection before the real answer.

jokes.text: I got so sucked into trying to repair you that I became the American auto industry, failing to recognize that you can't fix a Lemon.
jokes.setup: Jack is blaming Liz for his career stagnation and searching for an analogy.
jokes.punchline: He uses 'Lemon' both as a car industry term (defective product) and as Liz's last name — a double meaning that lands as both a burn and a pun.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best constructed jokes. 'You can't fix a Lemon' works simultaneously as: (1) the auto industry term for a defective vehicle, (2) Liz's last name, (3) a commentary on Jack's failure to improve Liz. The American auto industry analogy is apt (trying to fix something fundamentally broken), and the punchline arrives with perfect timing. Highly quotable. The line earns its wordplay because it builds to it rather than announcing it.

jokes.text: This show is her life. She hasn't got much going on. She threw a birthday party for her TV.
jokes.setup: Pete is defending Liz from being fired by Jack (in a flashback).
jokes.punchline: His defense of Liz includes the damning detail that she threw a birthday party for her television — confirming her loneliness while arguing for her employment.
jokes.explanation: The birthday party for the TV is an inspired specific detail — it's both pathetically funny and weirdly touching as a character note. Pete's defense inadvertently makes the case against Liz while intending to save her.

jokes.text: The important thing is that I fire someone... Pete.
jokes.setup: Jack is determined to fire someone as a show of authority after Pete argues for Liz.
jokes.punchline: He fires Pete — the man who just defended Liz — as a compromise.
jokes.explanation: The pause before 'Pete' is doing maximum structural work. The audience anticipates Liz; Jack fires Pete. It's a perfect misdirection with strong character integration — Jack's corporate logic (someone must be fired) trumps any personal loyalty. The pause is the punchline.

jokes.text: You tried to fire me? And then a week later, you're like, 'oh, I want to mentor you.' 'Unlikely friendship.'
jokes.setup: Liz has just learned from the flashback that Jack originally planned to fire her.
jokes.punchline: 'Unlikely friendship' — she air-quotes the TV trope that describes her relationship with Jack, calling out the cliché of their own story.
jokes.explanation: Liz calling their relationship an 'unlikely friendship' (in air quotes) is the show being meta about its own premise. It's also character-specific — Liz's media literacy lets her see their dynamic as a TV trope.

jokes.text: Paul, do you think I'd be a good mother? / Of course not. And I'd be a terrible father. I mean, what if we had a child that was prettier than us? We'd have to leave it in a desert.
jokes.setup: Jenna asks her equally theatrical boyfriend Paul if she'd be a good mother.
jokes.punchline: Paul agrees she'd be bad, adds he'd be a terrible father, and suggests they'd abandon a prettier child in a desert.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'what if we had a child that was prettier than us? We'd have to leave it in a desert' is both outrageous and logically consistent within the narcissistic framework of both characters. Paul and Jenna are perfectly matched in their vanity and dysfunction. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Right now, it's between 'Frisbeeface' and 'Glock,' gender irrelevant.
jokes.setup: Jenna says one upside of having a baby is that everyone would talk about her 'crazy name choice.'
jokes.punchline: The finalists are 'Frisbeeface' and 'Glock' — the 'gender irrelevant' addendum implying she hasn't gendered either name.
jokes.explanation: 'Frisbeeface' and 'Glock' are both excellent celebrity baby name parodies. 'Frisbeeface' is purely absurd; 'Glock' is a weapon — both would indeed generate outrage. 'Gender irrelevant' is the perfect deadpan tag. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: I love you, Jenna Maroney. I want to hogtie you and hide you in the luggage compartment of a Greyhound bus with just a bowl of dirty water.
jokes.setup: Paul is declaring his love for Jenna.
jokes.punchline: His love declaration includes the desire to hogtie her and hide her in a bus luggage compartment with a bowl of dirty water — framed as a romantic gesture.
jokes.explanation: An outstanding joke. The Greyhound bus luggage compartment is so specific and unglamorous that it's perfect — this isn't a luxury kidnapping fantasy, it's a bus. 'A bowl of dirty water' as the only provision is the perfect detail. The structure works because Paul delivers this as a love declaration, not a threat. Character integration is near-perfect — only Paul/Jenna's relationship would treat this as romance.

jokes.text: Break's over, Paul. Crew meeting in Lady Chantarelle's office. He's pissed.
jokes.setup: Paul and Jenna are having an intimate moment.
jokes.punchline: Paul is called away to a crew meeting in 'Lady Chantarelle's office' — an absurd name for whoever is running their performance world.
jokes.explanation: 'Lady Chantarelle' is a funny name for an authority figure in Paul's performance world, and 'He's pissed' with the gendered pronoun adds another comedic layer about Lady Chantarelle's gender identity.

jokes.text: Whazzup! You've reached Dennis' voicemail. 'How you doing?' Get out of here, Joey. I'm recording my voicemail message.
jokes.setup: Liz hears the voicemail she left Dennis.
jokes.punchline: Dennis's voicemail recording features a 'Whazzup!' (2000s cultural artifact), a Friends reference, and he's apparently recording it in front of someone named Joey — revealing the cheap cultural references that define his personality.
jokes.explanation: A tight character snapshot — Dennis's voicemail is a time capsule of faded pop culture references assembled without self-awareness. 'Get out of here, Joey' implies someone else is present during the recording, which adds visual chaos.

jokes.text: Good evening, sir. I'm Chris Hansen with Dateline NBC. Can I ask you what you're doing here tonight? / Yeah, I'm here to boff some chick named Mary. / Hey... threesome? / How about it, huh? / It's Tonya, right?
jokes.setup: Dennis is confronted by Chris Hansen in a To Catch a Predator-style sting.
jokes.punchline: Dennis immediately admits his purpose, then tries to include Hansen in a threesome, then gets the woman's name wrong — three escalating failures.
jokes.explanation: Excellent character comedy for Dennis. The escalation from admission to threesome proposition to name error is perfectly structured. 'It's Tonya, right?' as the button implies he doesn't even know the intended victim — he's both criminal and incompetent. Chris Hansen as a real person adds satirical punch.

jokes.text: Chew and screw! Run, dummy! / Ah! Damn it, Dennis! I checked a coat.
jokes.setup: Dennis is being confronted by Hansen and flees.
jokes.punchline: He calls it 'Chew and screw' — a dine-and-dash variation — and Liz's main concern is her checked coat.
jokes.explanation: 'Chew and screw' is a funny coinage for fleeing mid-meal. Liz's complaint about the coat is a perfect character-specific reaction — her practical concerns override the more pressing legal issue.

jokes.text: But you called me, Liz. / Oh, whatever. / 'Cause down deep, you still got all kinds of queer feelings for me. That's why I knew someday you'd be all vulnerable from a gas leak or a coma or a super period.
jokes.setup: Liz dismisses Dennis; he insists she has feelings for him.
jokes.punchline: He predicts her vulnerability would come from 'a gas leak or a coma or a super period' — the escalation from plausible to absurd is the joke.
jokes.explanation: 'A super period' as the third item in a list of vulnerability triggers is inspired. Dennis has apparently spent years cataloging the conditions under which Liz might call him. 'Gas leak' is funny because it's exactly what happened. The specificity of 'super period' elevates this significantly.

jokes.text: I'm a Duffy, Liz and us Duffys, we didn't give up when we got kicked out of Ireland. We didn't give up when America sent us back. And we didn't give up when Ireland then just set us adrift on a log, all right?
jokes.setup: Dennis makes a speech about Duffy family persistence.
jokes.punchline: The family history escalates from 'kicked out of Ireland' to 'America sent us back' to 'Ireland set us adrift on a log' — each return more humiliating and the last medieval in its punishment.
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke with perfect escalation structure. Three beats, each worse than the last: kicked out, sent back, set adrift on a log. The log is the genius move — it's so primitive and final. 'All right?' as the tag implies Dennis finds this inspiring rather than mortifying. Exceptional character integration for Dennis — his pride in a catastrophic heritage is exactly who he is.

jokes.text: And out on the Plaza, a bird landed on my apple. I thought he was gonna eat it, but he just sat there. What's next? A different bird landing on a different apple?
jokes.setup: Kenneth is enthusiastically summarizing everything wonderful that happened today.
jokes.punchline: His greatest wonder — equal in excitement to Tracy coming back and the best show ever — is a bird that sat on his apple and didn't eat it.
jokes.explanation: Kenneth's childlike wonder at the bird is perfectly calibrated. 'What's next? A different bird landing on a different apple?' as a vision of future marvels is both absurd and endearing. Only Kenneth treats this as equivalent to professional triumphs. 'A different bird on a different apple' as the sci-fi imagination of escalation is inspired.

jokes.text: I even called a woman's basketball team 'Nappy-headed hos,' but apparently, I'm allowed to talk like that. Why?
jokes.setup: Tracy is trying to make people hate him and has pulled out the most infamous racial slur incident in recent sports history (Don Imus).
jokes.punchline: Tracy's version of the slur doesn't create controversy because — apparently — he's allowed to say it, and he's genuinely confused why.
jokes.explanation: Smart joke about racial double standards in comedy and media — Tracy's confusion about why he's allowed to say something Don Imus was fired for is a genuine piece of social commentary wrapped in character comedy.

jokes.text: Brian Williams sure gets close to you when he talks. Very feminine energy.
jokes.setup: Hank casually mentions meeting Brian Williams
jokes.punchline: His observation about Williams's proximity and 'feminine energy' is a very specific and strange character read delivered with complete folksy sincerity
jokes.explanation: The Brian Williams proximity joke is a great Hank moment — his odd observation about a real person, delivered as a normal conversational aside. 'Very feminine energy' as a characterization of Brian Williams is funny in its specificity and oddness.

jokes.text: You know, he just likes to learn his lines in the bathroom and communicate by phone. Actors, am I right?
jokes.setup: Hank Hooper wants to meet Tracy; Liz must explain Tracy's absence.
jokes.punchline: Liz invents an absurd excuse — Tracy learns lines in bathrooms and only communicates by phone — and delivers it with false confidence, then appeals to the universal exasperation of 'Actors, am I right?'
jokes.explanation: Liz's bad improvised excuse paired with a conspiratorial 'Actors, am I right?' to Hank is a fun character moment — she's terrible at lying but commits fully.

jokes.text: He is here. You know, he just likes to learn his lines in the bathroom and communicate by phone. Actors, am I right?
jokes.setup: Hank Hooper arrives and there's no Tracy; Liz has to cover
jokes.punchline: Liz's improvised lie — that Tracy learns lines in the bathroom and communicates only by phone — is presented with a 'that's just actors!' shrug, which Hank apparently accepts
jokes.explanation: Good workplace comedy — Liz's desperation improvisation is plausible enough to be funny and ridiculous enough to be absurd. 'Actors, am I right?' as a bonding deflection is perfectly timed.

jokes.text: I'm just kidding! I mean, look at March of the Penguins. Who was in that?
jokes.setup: Hank is talking about the Screen Actors Guild being nutjobs but necessary.
jokes.punchline: He cites March of the Penguins — a documentary with no human actors — as evidence that you can make movies without the Screen Actors Guild.
jokes.explanation: March of the Penguins as the example of actor-free filmmaking is perfectly Hank — he's not wrong (there are no human actors), but the logic is comically literal. Character-specific folksy wisdom.

jokes.text: Oh, excuse me, miss. How much is a lap dance? I'm a little light on cash, but I have a PayPal account.
jokes.setup: Kenneth enters the strip club with Liz and Tracy.
jokes.punchline: Kenneth politely inquires about prices and offers PayPal as an alternative to cash — treating the transaction with his signature formal innocence.
jokes.explanation: Kenneth's formal politeness in a strip club ('excuse me, miss') combined with the practical problem-solving of offering PayPal is perfect character comedy. He treats the transaction like ordering at a restaurant.

jokes.text: No daddy stuff. / I know you've been molested. That's how we all got here, but I don't want to hear about it.
jokes.setup: A stripper is moved to tears by Tracy's Oscar-winning movie and begins sharing personal revelations.
jokes.punchline: Tracy cuts off her backstory with 'I know you've been molested. That's how we all got here, but I don't want to hear about it.'
jokes.explanation: Dark and uncomfortable. Tracy's callousness functions as character comedy — he's not trying to be cruel, he's genuinely just trying to avoid the inspiration moment. The 'That's how we all got here' is a brutal generalization delivered with zero irony.

jokes.text: But I wasn't even supposed to say that. The line was, 'Shereen, I hope Dr. Mogutu has good news about my endoscopy,' but I couldn't get it right, so they told me to improv.
jokes.setup: A young man credits Tracy's Oscar-winning line 'I invent my tomorrow' with inspiring him to join the Navy.
jokes.punchline: Tracy reveals the line was an accident — he couldn't learn a line about an endoscopy, so the director told him to improv.
jokes.explanation: Excellent deconstruction of celebrity inspiration. The specific detail of the original line (endoscopy, Dr. Mogutu, Shereen) makes the accidental-improv explanation hilarious. It satirizes both Hollywood sentimentality and Tracy's incompetence simultaneously — and the Navy recruit is still inspired even after learning it was an accident.

jokes.text: There are tears falling on her boobies, Liz Lemon.
jokes.setup: The stripper is crying while dancing.
jokes.punchline: Tracy reports the situation to Liz with his signature blunt sincerity.
jokes.explanation: 'Boobies' delivered with complete sincerity in a crisis report format is very Tracy. The specificity of tears on boobies as the marker of failure is both sad and funny.

jokes.text: Fine. I'll get you when you're sleeping. It's not rape if neither party really wants it.
jokes.setup: Kenneth refuses Jenna's proposition to father her child.
jokes.punchline: Jenna threatens to do it while he sleeps, then provides a legal/ethical justification that makes zero sense.
jokes.explanation: The darkly absurd logic of 'not rape if neither party wants it' is both wrong and internally consistent in Jenna's moral universe. The confidence of the delivery makes it funnier than the actual content.

jokes.text: You're back. / Yeah, and this is my front. / Thanks for setting me up with another classic quote.
jokes.setup: Liz tells Tracy he's 'back.'
jokes.punchline: Tracy responds 'Yeah, and this is my front' — a literal/figure of speech pun — then Liz thanks him for the 'classic quote,' making the meta-acknowledgment the button.
jokes.explanation: The back/front wordplay is simple but well-delivered, and Liz's 'thanks for setting me up' makes it meta — she's in the room with Tracy and anticipates his puns so well she's already critiquing them. Clean and efficient.

jokes.text: Look at Roman Polanski. / No, thank you. / Or Elia Kazan. He told the government his friends were communists, then got a standing ovation at the Oscars. That's crazy. A man named 'Elia.' That's a giraffe's name.
jokes.setup: Liz is trying to explain how celebrities maintain goodwill even after terrible behavior.
jokes.punchline: Elia Kazan gets a standing ovation despite being an informant; Tracy's objection isn't to the behavior but to the name — 'That's a giraffe's name.'
jokes.explanation: 'Elia' is a giraffe's name is a sublime non-sequitur. The Kazan joke is sharp Hollywood-history satire; Tracy's objection being to the name rather than the behavior is perfect character comedy. The pivot from serious (Communist informant/Oscar) to absurd (giraffe) is exactly 30 Rock's register.

jokes.text: You know, when you think about it, the only celebrities who completely undo their goodwill are the murderers. John Wilkes Booth, Phil Spector, OJ Simpson, who texted me earlier today.
jokes.setup: Liz is trying to help Tracy find a way to destroy his goodwill.
jokes.punchline: The list of celebrity goodwill-destroyers ends with OJ Simpson, who 'texted me earlier today' — Liz has apparently been in contact with OJ.
jokes.explanation: The list works through legitimate historical examples (Booth, Spector) to OJ, then the casual 'who texted me earlier today' lands as a perfect tag. Liz having a texting relationship with OJ Simpson is completely unexpected and funny precisely for its mundane casualness.

jokes.text: 100th episode, 100 hours of comedy. Minus the commercials. 20 hours of comedy.
jokes.setup: Pete announces the 100th episode milestone.
jokes.punchline: The triumphant 100 hours becomes 20 hours once commercials are removed — a deflating but accurate observation.
jokes.explanation: The mathematical deflation is a quick and efficient joke. The structure (big number, qualifier, small number) works as a three-beat in two sentences.

jokes.text: Look, Liz, if this is gonna work out between you and me, you should know my tarantula sleeps on my face.
jokes.setup: Dennis is negotiating the terms of getting back together with Liz.
jokes.punchline: His key disclosure is that his tarantula sleeps on his face — offered as a relationship dealbreaker warning.
jokes.explanation: This is the kind of specific Dennis detail that makes him a great recurring character. 'Tarantula sleeps on my face' is an absurd dealbreaker to lead with — not 'I'm in a database' or 'I have no job' — but a face-sleeping spider. Perfectly calibrated to his chaos.

jokes.text: Gas has no effect on me at all. When I was growing up, my school, Gerry Cooney Elementary, it was right next to a gas works in Queens. It ventilated into the cafeteria. We got a big settlement from the city. Our parents voted to spend it on a boat that the families could share, but then that sank.
jokes.setup: Dennis explains why gas doesn't affect him.
jokes.punchline: His childhood gas exposure story escalates: the school got a settlement, the community spent it on a boat, the boat sank.
jokes.explanation: The escalation structure is excellent — each detail is worse than the last. Naming the school after Gerry Cooney (Queens boxer) is a loving specific detail. The settlement-spent-on-a-boat-that-sank is a perfect disaster escalation. Establishes Dennis's entire world of poorly-managed communal tragedy.

jokes.text: But you know what? I'm still smart enough to know that I'll never do better than you, Liz Lemon, 'cause you're a cook in the bedroom and a whore in the kitchen.
jokes.setup: Dennis is making a heartfelt argument for why Liz should be with him.
jokes.punchline: He inverts the classic phrase 'cook in the kitchen and a whore in the bedroom' — either through stupidity or deliberate subversion.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's most quotable lines. The inversion is either stupidity or a revelation about Liz — she's competent at cooking but treats the kitchen as her place of transgression, and is dutiful and responsible in bed. Dennis is accidentally profound. The 'never do better than you' framing makes it a bizarrely touching declaration. Perfect Dennis.

jokes.text: Let's rock, Duffy.
jokes.setup: Dennis is about to head somewhere with himself (possibly to gather more Duffys).
jokes.punchline: He says 'Let's rock, Duffy' to himself — the absurdity of self-addressed encouragement.
jokes.explanation: A brief, self-contained character beat. Dennis rallying himself is inherently funny given his circumstances. Economy of 9 for four words.

jokes.text: You're 87 years old? My God, I'm outstanding.
jokes.setup: Future Jack appears and reveals he's from 35 years in the future.
jokes.punchline: Jack computes that this means he's 87 and his immediate reaction is pride at his own continued vitality.
jokes.explanation: Jack's first reaction to learning he's 87 is not surprise, not existential crisis, but narcissistic pride — 'My God, I'm outstanding.' Pure Jack. The line does a lot of character work very efficiently.

jokes.text: This is how everyone talked in the '80s. This is how Reagan talked.
jokes.setup: Present Jack questions Past Jack's speech pattern
jokes.punchline: Past Jack defends his 1980s dialogue by invoking Reagan — implying both that Reagan spoke in movie-trailer clichés and that this was normal
jokes.explanation: Good character-specific political joke — Jack's admiration for Reagan is well-established, so the implication that Reagan spoke in 80s action-movie clichés is a pointed commentary on Jack's political hero worship.

jokes.text: Well, that's redundant. All pregnancies are hysterical. They're started by penises.
jokes.setup: Jenna is diagnosed with a hysterical pregnancy
jokes.punchline: The doctor redefines 'hysterical' — 'all pregnancies are hysterical' because penises are inherently ridiculous
jokes.explanation: 'All pregnancies are hysterical. They're started by penises.' is an excellent wordplay joke exploiting the dual meaning of 'hysterical' (medical/emotional). The two-sentence structure is perfectly economical and the punchline lands cleanly.

jokes.text: Mr. Jordan, I refuse to accept this is happening. You leaving is as crazy to me as evolution, or a woman's right to choose her haircut.
jokes.setup: Kenneth is trying to stop Tracy from leaving
jokes.punchline: His list of 'crazy things' includes evolution (funny because Kenneth is from a religious rural background and may literally not believe in it) and 'a woman's right to choose her haircut' — an extremely specific patriarchal concern
jokes.explanation: A brilliant Kenneth character joke. His list of things he finds crazy — evolution and women choosing haircuts — is both character-specific (Kenneth's conservative, possibly creationist worldview) and escalates from the grand (evolution) to the absurdly petty (haircut autonomy). The specificity of 'haircut' rather than any bigger choice is what makes it exceptional.

jokes.text: You should shoot me... / I should shoot you... / —on the roof of 30 Rock! / —on the roof of 30 Rock! / I only ask one thing, sir. Make it quick. / I cannot promise you that, Ken. I'm a horrible shot.
jokes.setup: Tracy and Kenneth simultaneously arrive at the same bad solution to Tracy's problem
jokes.punchline: Both reaching 'on the roof of 30 Rock' simultaneously, then Kenneth's noble resignation and Tracy's honest disclaimer about his marksmanship
jokes.explanation: The synchronized realization is excellent structure; Kenneth's acceptance ('make it quick') and Tracy's practical problem ('I'm a horrible shot') are the perfect dual punchlines. The dark absurdism of this solution is peak Tracy/Kenneth dynamic. The structural choice to have them say the same thing simultaneously is a formal comedy technique executed well.

jokes.text: You have grandchildren and a gorgeous Polyblasian wife. That's a new race that emerges in 2030. They're incredible.
jokes.setup: Future Jack is describing what awaits current Jack if he takes the right path.
jokes.punchline: 'Polyblasian' is a made-up future race; the delivery of 'They're incredible' as a proud aside is the button.
jokes.explanation: 'Polyblasian' is an excellent invented racial portmanteau. The specificity of 2030 as the emergence date, and 'They're incredible' as an ethnic group review, is both funny and sharp.

jokes.text: What happened to Avery? / Oh, you'll see. It's hilarious.
jokes.setup: Jack asks about his current wife Avery when told about his Polyblasian future wife.
jokes.punchline: Future Jack says Avery's fate is 'hilarious' — which is either terrible or genuinely funny, and he won't reveal it.
jokes.explanation: The evasive 'You'll see. It's hilarious' about Avery is a great joke about narrative misdirection — and also sets up a future plot point while being funny in itself.

jokes.text: You'll spearhead GE's development of the electric vagina. You won't be married, but you'll have a house with a lot of glass, and it's cold. And you'll own the Buffalo Bills. / You didn't say it was the Bills.
jokes.setup: Sideways Jack is selling the corporate success timeline.
jokes.punchline: The achievements (electric vagina, glass house, NFL team) culminate in the Bills — the least glamorous NFL franchise — as the reveal that deflates the whole pitch.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The 'electric vagina' as GE product is inspired (GE's product range is a running joke on 30 Rock). Then the cold glass house as a status symbol. Then 'you'll own the Buffalo Bills' — and Jack's response 'You didn't say it was the Bills' is the perfect reaction. The Bills as shorthand for NFL failure is universal enough to land hard. The structure (amazing, amazing, terrible revelation) is flawlessly executed.

jokes.text: Right now, Liz Lemon is downstairs about to sign a lease with Dennis Duffy. If she does that, you'll lose her. In three years, they'll be married and living in Jacksonville, Florida, where he operates an unlicensed alligator park.
jokes.setup: Future Jack is warning current Jack about losing Liz to Dennis.
jokes.punchline: The worst possible outcome is Dennis running 'an unlicensed alligator park' in Jacksonville — highly specific and deeply plausible for Dennis.
jokes.explanation: 'Unlicensed alligator park' in Jacksonville is perfect for Dennis. It's not a legitimate business, it's in one of the more unglamorous cities, and alligators imply both Florida and danger. The detail is specific enough to feel researched but absurd enough to be clearly invented.

jokes.text: No, I don't care. I'm tired of saving her. To quote Liz Lemon, 'Opposite!' / You'd be saving yourself.
jokes.setup: Jack refuses to help Liz again
jokes.punchline: Jack quotes Liz's own catchphrase 'Opposite!' back to Future Jack; Future Jack uses it to redirect
jokes.explanation: A functional callback that uses Liz's verbal tic against Jack. The structure is clean but not among the episode's most inventive moments.

jokes.text: Jacksonville? Her hair can't handle that humidity.
jokes.setup: Future Jack warns about Liz moving to Jacksonville with Dennis.
jokes.punchline: Jack's primary objection to Jacksonville is Liz's hair and humidity — not the alligator park or the marriage.
jokes.explanation: Beautiful joke. Jack's concern for Liz is expressed entirely through her hair and the Florida humidity — which is both absurd (that's his objection?) and reveals how intimately he knows her. The deflection from the genuine emotional stakes to a practical hair concern is perfectly Jack.

jokes.text: We're obviously all thinking it, so I'm just gonna say it. We're gonna have sex with each other, right? / Yeah, we are. / Oh, my!
jokes.setup: The three alternate Jacks and real Jack are all together in a room.
jokes.punchline: One Jack voices what they're all thinking — they're going to have sex — and the others immediately agree, with Kenneth reacting with 'Oh, my!'
jokes.explanation: A genuine shock comedy moment — the implication of narcissistic self-sex among alternate selves is unexpected, audacious, and then Kenneth's 'Oh, my!' is the perfect reaction. The logic is internally consistent (Jack IS attracted to himself) and it's committed to fully. Genuinely daring comedy.

jokes.text: No. / Just sign it, dummy. It's a receipt for some lez pants you bought or whatever. / No.
jokes.setup: Jack is stopping Liz from signing the lease; Dennis tries to reframe it.
jokes.punchline: Dennis calls it 'a receipt for some lez pants' — the improvised lie is both specific and absurd.
jokes.explanation: 'Lez pants' as an improvised category of clothing is a funny Dennis-specific invention. The 'or whatever' dismissiveness sells it.

jokes.text: If you have a problem, I will fight you, Dennis. / That wouldn't be very fair. I'm only trained to fight four or more men at a time. There are three more of me upstairs, and I'd be happy to go get them.
jokes.setup: Jack threatens to fight Dennis.
jokes.punchline: Dennis says he's only trained for four or more opponents, then offers to get three more of himself (the Duffys) to make it a fair fight.
jokes.explanation: The combat training detail (four or more opponents) is absurdist and specific. The callback to 'three more of me upstairs' plants actual Duffys in the building while escalating the family mythology established earlier. The logic of offering to make a fight fair by fetching more of yourself is perfect Dennis comedy.

jokes.text: Hands off the jacket, all right? It's from Amar'e Stoudemire's eveningwear collection.
jokes.setup: Dennis is being grabbed during the altercation.
jokes.punchline: He defends his jacket by citing Amar'e Stoudemire's (NBA player) eveningwear collection — an unlikely designer for a Queens guy.
jokes.explanation: Amar'e Stoudemire is a specific enough NBA player to be funny, and 'eveningwear collection' as a fashion category for a basketball player is absurd but plausible enough (athletes do have clothing lines). Dennis's fashion pride in the middle of a brawl is perfectly him.

jokes.text: Somebody sabotaged the gas line. People could've died or had fights.
jokes.setup: The gas leak is revealed to have been sabotage.
jokes.punchline: 'People could've died or had fights' — the equivalence of death and fights is a casually deflating scale of consequences.
jokes.explanation: The casual equivalence of death and fights as equally weighted outcomes is excellent deadpan comedy. Economy of 9 for a very short line.

jokes.text: It was you. / What are you, mad at me, Liz? Huh? I did it for love.
jokes.setup: The sabotage is revealed; everyone looks at Dennis.
jokes.punchline: Dennis admits it immediately, explaining he 'did it for love' — his romantic motivation is sabotaging a gas line.
jokes.explanation: 'I did it for love' as a gas-line sabotage defense is peak Dennis. He's not embarrassed; he's defending the motive as if the method is perfectly reasonable. The casualness of the admission is the comedy.

jokes.text: If I ever see you again, I'll kill you. / Please. You'll be back.
jokes.setup: Liz kicks Dennis out definitively
jokes.punchline: Dennis's confident prediction that she'll be back — delivered with complete ease after being threatened with death — is the joke
jokes.explanation: A functional character beat — Dennis's unshakeable confidence is his defining trait. 'Please. You'll be back.' after a death threat is good character comedy, though less crafted than his bigger jokes this episode.

jokes.text: When TGS gets cancelled, I mean if, when TGS gets cancelled, we need to talk about your future.
jokes.setup: Hank is trying to be diplomatic about TGS's future.
jokes.punchline: He catches his slip ('I mean if') and then repeats 'when TGS gets cancelled' anyway — the Freudian slip confirmed.
jokes.explanation: The self-correction followed by the same slip is a well-worn comedy structure, but executed well here because Hank's folksy obliviousness makes the repetition feel authentic rather than calculated.

jokes.text: I'm not gonna be held back by some uterus turd.
jokes.setup: Jenna has been considering motherhood; now she's abandoning it for a talk show.
jokes.punchline: She refers to a baby as 'a uterus turd' — reductive to an extreme, delivered with complete conviction.
jokes.explanation: 'Uterus turd' is one of the most original and shocking phrases in the episode. It's disgusting, reductive, and perfectly Jenna — her rejection of motherhood delivered in the most visceral possible terms. The casualness of delivery is key. Highly quotable and completely character-specific.

jokes.text: Do you have any idea how much paperwork I would have to do if you shot Kenneth?
jokes.setup: Jack arrives on the roof to stop Tracy from shooting Kenneth
jokes.punchline: Jack's objection to Kenneth's murder is not ethical — it's the paperwork involved. His bureaucratic concern for Kenneth's life is the joke.
jokes.explanation: A great Jack joke — his concern for Kenneth is expressed entirely through professional inconvenience. 'Do you have any idea how much paperwork I would have to do?' as a murder deterrent is both darkly funny and perfectly in character. His relationship with Kenneth is expressed through institutional inconvenience rather than human feeling. Earns the score.

jokes.text: For some reason, I'm starting to rethink this, sir. / We all have doubt, k-tel records. But we made a decision. And we'll look stupid if we don't follow through.
jokes.setup: Kenneth is about to be shot by Tracy on the roof.
jokes.punchline: Tracy's reassurance to Kenneth includes calling him 'k-tel records' — a completely random nickname — and arguing they must continue because backing out 'would look stupid.'
jokes.explanation: 'K-tel records' as a nickname is a wonderful random reference. Tracy's logic that they must follow through because otherwise they'd 'look stupid' (after agreeing to shoot someone on a roof) is beautifully absurd.

jokes.text: For some reason, I'm starting to rethink this, sir. / We all have doubt, K-tel records. But we made a decision. And we'll look stupid if we don't follow through.
jokes.setup: Kenneth is having second thoughts about being shot on the roof
jokes.punchline: Tracy's argument for following through is 'we'll look stupid if we don't' — treating embarrassment as a worse outcome than Kenneth being shot
jokes.explanation: Tracy's motivation for following through — social embarrassment — is funnier than any other justification. 'We'll look stupid if we don't' as a reason to shoot someone is perfect dark absurdism. The 'K-tel records' as Kenneth's nickname is also a funny throwaway.

jokes.text: I only ask one thing, sir. Make it quick. / I cannot promise you that, Ken. I'm a horrible shot.
jokes.setup: Kenneth accepts being shot and asks for mercy.
jokes.punchline: Tracy honestly confesses he can't promise a quick death because he's a bad shot.
jokes.explanation: Perfect two-beat joke. Kenneth's selfless request (make it quick) is met with Tracy's completely honest and practical response that undermines the mercy of it. 'I cannot promise you that, Ken. I'm a horrible shot' is delivered with such sincere regret that it's both dark and touching.

jokes.text: Doesn't matter how big a movie star you are, even if you have the kind of career where you walked away from a blockbuster franchise or worked with Meryl Streep or Anthony Hopkins, made important movies about things like civil rights or Pearl Harbor, stole films with supporting roles and then turned around and blew them away on Broadway. None of that will matter once you do television. You could win every award in sight and be the biggest thing on the small screen, and you'll still get laughed out of the Vanity Fair Oscar party by Greg Kinnear.
jokes.setup: Jack is arguing that doing TV will instantly destroy Tracy's film credibility.
jokes.punchline: The list of prestigious film accomplishments ends with 'laughed out of the Vanity Fair Oscar party by Greg Kinnear' — the most devastating possible humiliation.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's great sustained jokes and a genuine piece of Hollywood satire. The list of achievements escalates beautifully, each one more impressive than the last. The kicker — 'laughed out by Greg Kinnear' — is genius because Kinnear is a perfectly calibrated choice: he's respected but not a titan, which makes the humiliation total. This is also meta-commentary on 30 Rock itself (and Tina Fey's own career). The 'Pearl Harbor' inclusion is a knowing wink. Exceptional.

jokes.text: I'm sorry, folks. While we were working on the gas line, we somehow broke the elevator. She's an old building.
jokes.setup: The gas is cleared and everyone can head back upstairs.
jokes.punchline: Trying to fix one problem, the maintenance crew created a new one — they broke the elevator.
jokes.explanation: Functional comedy of escalating building problems — creates a reason for the stairwell scene. Not a standout joke but serves a narrative purpose.

jokes.text: Excuse me. The elevators are out. Do you know how-- / Shut up, Garkle.
