jokes.setup: Someone tries to ask Jack for directions in the stairwell.
jokes.punchline: Jack cuts them off mid-sentence with 'Shut up, Garkle' — a name, implying he knows this person, making the dismissal more personal.
jokes.explanation: 'Garkle' as a name is inherently funny — it's an ugly, specific word. Cutting off someone by name mid-sentence is perfect Jack aggression. Economy: maximum.

jokes.text: Well, if it isn't Jack and Kenneth and Tracy and Liz. Hey, I have a bone to pick with the four of you. / Screw, Williams! / Hey, get out of my home! / Sorry, recurring hobos.
jokes.setup: The group runs into Brian Williams in the stairwell.
jokes.punchline: Brian Williams has a complaint for them; Jack tells him to screw off; he responds 'get out of my home'; Liz apologizes to 'recurring hobos.'
jokes.explanation: Brian Williams is a perfectly calibrated NBC cameo — the dignity of an actual news anchor being told to 'screw off' and responding by claiming the stairwell as his home is absurd. 'Recurring hobos' as Liz's explanation is the button. The whole sequence works because of the compressed absurdity.

jokes.text: I'm back, everybody. You're welcome... For the adventure... My absence... Whew... Provided.
jokes.setup: Tracy returns to the TGS studio for the show.
jokes.punchline: His return speech fragments into increasingly incoherent pause-filler — 'you're welcome... for the adventure... my absence... whew... provided' — suggesting he's either lost his speech or improvising badly.
jokes.explanation: The fragmenting non-speech is a great Tracy bit — his triumphant return announcement trailing off into nothing captures his character's grandiosity and incoherence simultaneously.

jokes.text: I'm back, everybody. You're welcome... For the adventure... My absence... Whew... Provided.
jokes.setup: Tracy arrives at the show 30 seconds before airtime
jokes.punchline: His triumphant return speech is progressively less coherent — he trails off mid-sentence and has to reconstruct what he's thanking them for: 'the adventure my absence... provided'
jokes.explanation: Tracy's exhausted, fragmented speech is good character comedy — the pauses and self-corrections reveal he's completely depleted but committed to the triumphant return bit. The structure of the reconstructed sentence ('the adventure... my absence... provided') is funny in how it limps to completion.

jokes.text: Let's meet our contestants. Dr. Steven Poop is a homemaker and a centaur.
jokes.setup: TGS begins its 100th episode show — we hear the game show cold open.
jokes.punchline: The first contestant is 'Dr. Steven Poop' who is both a homemaker and a centaur.
jokes.explanation: 'Dr. Steven Poop' is a perfect comedy name (the 'Dr.' before 'Poop' is doing enormous work). The straight-faced announcement that the doctor is also a centaur — treated as a normal demographic detail — is pure absurdist comedy. Extremely quotable.

jokes.text: You did it. You're picked up for a million more episodes.
jokes.setup: Someone tells TGS they've been picked up.
jokes.punchline: 'A million more episodes' is an absurd number — not renewed, not cancelled, but picked up for a million.
jokes.explanation: A quick absurdist throwaway — the specific number (a million) is the joke. Functional but not elaborate.

jokes.text: Am I back in Vietnam?
jokes.setup: The chaos and noise of the show going on around them.
jokes.punchline: A character is so disoriented by the show chaos that they believe they've returned to Vietnam.
jokes.explanation: A brief throwaway joke — the Vietnam flashback gag is well-worn and earns a modest chuckle here from context. Not particularly crafted.

jokes.text: The Grimace Foundation, Jeremy. Keeping milkshakes purple for over a million years.
jokes.setup: Tracy is playing a game show contestant; asked what charity he's playing for
jokes.punchline: 'The Grimace Foundation' — honoring the McDonald's character Grimace — dedicated to keeping milkshakes purple, apparently for a million years
jokes.explanation: The Grimace Foundation is an inspired invention. 'Keeping milkshakes purple' as a charitable mission is absurd but internally consistent with Grimace's character. 'For over a million years' implies prehistoric milkshake conservation. Tracy's commitment to this as his charity of choice is perfect character comedy.

jokes.text: What charity are you playing for? / The Grimace Foundation, Jeremy. Keeping milkshakes purple for over a million years.
jokes.setup: A game show asks contestants what charity they're playing for.
jokes.punchline: 'The Grimace Foundation — Keeping milkshakes purple for over a million years' is an invented charity with a mission statement that makes no sense.
jokes.explanation: Outstanding joke. Grimace (the McDonald's character) as the basis for a foundation, with the mission of keeping milkshakes purple 'for over a million years' (McDonald's has only existed for decades, not a million years) is absurdist comedy at a very high level. The specificity and internal illogic are perfectly calibrated. One of the episode's top moments.

jokes.text: Tracy Jordan's doing TV again? / Clooney, Hanks. Actor emergency. Tracy Jordan's doing TV again. / I know, disappointing. / Take him off the official A-list. / Well, I don't have the password. Pitt's our webmaster. / Well, then, wake him up.
jokes.setup: We see the Hollywood establishment react to Tracy doing TV.
jokes.punchline: Clooney and Hanks treat it as an emergency; 'Brad Pitt is the A-list webmaster'; they'll wake him up to update the list.
jokes.explanation: This is the payoff to Jack's long speech about television destroying film careers — and it's handled by real Hollywood A-listers being named. 'Pitt's our webmaster' is inspired — the image of Brad Pitt maintaining the A-list database is absurd and perfectly bureaucratic. Waking him up for an emergency update is the button.

jokes.text: Oh, they're doing Pam again? Ugh.
jokes.setup: The Hollywood celebrities are watching TGS's 100th episode.
jokes.punchline: Even movie stars recognize and are exasperated by the Pam sketch repetition.
jokes.explanation: The Pam running gag pays off perfectly here. The fact that Hollywood celebrities recognize the Pam sketch by name and have the same 'ugh' reaction as any long-time viewer is a great structural callback that brings the episode's running gag to a satisfying close.

jokes.text: This may be the gas talking, but I was wrong about Dennis. You're the guy who never left.
jokes.setup: Liz appears to be having a genuine emotional moment with Jack.
jokes.punchline: 'This may be the gas talking' as a disclaimer before a sincere admission — attributing her honesty to chemical influence.
jokes.explanation: The callback to the gas as a truth-serum device is used for genuine emotional payoff. Liz attributing her sincerity to the gas (rather than accepting she means it) is quintessential Liz emotional deflection.

jokes.text: And this is definitely the gas talking, but I'd be a lot worse off if I'd never met you, Lemon, and I'm proud to have you as a mentee. I mean, look at you. Endangering the lives of hundreds of people for a show that TV Guide once called 'still on.' I framed that article.
jokes.setup: Jack returns the sentiment, also crediting the gas for his honesty.
jokes.punchline: His proud description of Liz includes 'endangering hundreds of lives for a show TV Guide called Still On' — and she framed that article.
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect closing joke for the emotional arc. 'Still On' as the only TV Guide review is a reference back to the episode's Wikipedia joke, escalated. 'She framed that article' is the button that's simultaneously sad and triumphant. The entire joke structure (gas disclaimer + genuine praise + devastating qualification + proud tag) is a masterwork of comedic structure. Highly quotable.

tmdb_overview: Chaos builds when bigwig Hank Hooper marks "TGS" for cancellation, yet Jack persuades him to let the staffers stage the show's 100th episode.
insight: 104 jokes in 49 minutes: 30 Rock hits peak density with character-driven escalation.
